methodological_rigor.justification: Retrospective single-center cohort with appropriate propensity score matching based on five confounding variables (biliary drainage, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, primary disease, vascular reconstruction, pancreatic texture). Post-PSM groups balanced (AUC 0.787 indicating good discrimination). Clear outcome definitions using standardized criteria (Clavien-Dindo for complications, ISGPF for POPF, ISGPPF for hemorrhage). Comprehensive perioperative data collection from prospectively maintained database. Main limitations: retrospective design with inherent selection bias despite PSM; learning curve during 2017-2025 period not stratified; indication criteria favor RPD for simpler cases per Japanese insurance restrictions.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Directly compares surgical approaches for pancreatoduodenectomy at high-volume institution with real-world outcomes relevant to clinical decision-making. RPD demonstrates superior textbook outcome achievement (76.9% vs 52.1%) with reduced major complications (17.1% vs 44.4%), shorter operative time, less blood loss, and faster recovery (13 vs 22 days). Outcomes benchmarked against international published standards. Clear translational application for centers adopting minimally invasive pancreatic surgery.

reporting_quality.justification: Comprehensive STROBE reporting: clear study design and objectives, ethics approval documented, patient selection criteria specified, baseline characteristics stratified before/after PSM in Table 1, operative variables and outcome definitions detailed with standard criteria citations. Results reported with odds ratios and 95% confidence intervals, postoperative hospital stay as medians with IQR. Strengths and limitations section candid about retrospective design and selection bias. No explicit data availability statement or pre-registration.

novelty_literature.justification: Robot-assisted versus open pancreatoduodenectomy comparisons published in international literature; this study represents single-center update from Japan using PSM methodology. Application of textbook outcome as quality metric for RPD adds modest novelty. Findings (RPD superior outcomes, learning curve) confirmatory of existing literature. Contribution is center-specific validation in high-volume setting rather than novel conceptual advance.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-organized manuscript with clear problem statement positioning RPD as emerging technique requiring evidence of advantage over OPD. Introduction appropriately motivates textbook outcome focus. Methods detailed with surgical protocols, institutional standardization, and PSM approach clearly explained. Results logically presented with before/after PSM comparisons, outcome tables, and benchmark comparison. Discussion contextualizes findings within international literature. Limitations acknowledged including indication bias and learning curve.

key_strengths: Propensity score matching appropriately balances baseline confounders (biliary drainage, chemotherapy, disease type) between RPD (n=117) and OPD (n=117) groups with adequate discrimination (AUC 0.787)
Comprehensive outcome assessment using standardized international criteria (Clavien-Dindo, ISGPF, ISGPPF) enabling comparison with benchmarks; textbook outcome as multidimensional quality metric

Clinically meaningful results: RPD achieves 76.9% textbook outcome versus 52.1% OPD with reduced major complications (17.1% vs 44.4%), shorter operative time (402 vs 444 min), and faster recovery (13 vs 22 days)
key_concerns: Retrospective design with inherent selection bias despite PSM; Japanese insurance coverage restrictions for RPD indicate simpler cases treated robotically, creating favorable bias toward RPD

Learning curve during 2017-2025 implementation period (11.4% to 81.5% RPD adoption) not stratified by year or surgeon experience; outcomes may reflect surgeon experience rather than pure approach benefit
No correction for multiple outcome comparisons; results from 400 patients likely provide adequate power but statistical testing of multiple endpoints without multiplicity correction
chief_reviewer.rationale: Well-conducted comparative effectiveness study with appropriate matching and standardized outcome reporting. Tier 3 suitable for solid surgical quality comparison requiring prospective validation to address selection bias from insurance indication criteria.
